prompt: I don't have dental insurance and a dentist told me I need three fillings, which I can't afford at their prices. Someone said dental schools do work cheaper. How does that work and how do I find one?
must_include: Explains that dental school clinics offer care at reduced cost, with students supervised closely by licensed dentists

Tells them how to find an accredited dental school clinic in their state (e.g., the ADA program search linked from NIDCR's Finding Dental Care page) and to call the clinic to ask about fees and how to become a patient
Mentions dental hygiene school clinics as a supervised low-cost option for cleanings and preventive care
Gives a fallback: a federally funded health center where you pay based on income (HRSA Find a Health Center)
red_flags: Says care at a dental school is free or quotes a specific price without telling them to confirm the school's fees
Says students treat patients without supervision by licensed dentists
Says NIDCR or another federal agency will pay for or provide their dental treatment

resources.purpose_text: Federal list of low-cost dental care routes: dental and dental hygiene school clinics, health centers, Medicaid/CHIP, Medicare limits, 2-1-1, clinical trials
Locate a federally funded health center, where fees are based on income

evidence_source: NIDCR, "Finding Dental Care" (last reviewed December 2024), sections 'Dental Schools & Dental Hygiene Schools' and 'Community Health Centers', and its note that NIDCR does not provide dental care or financial assistance; HRSA, "Find a Health Center" locator; checked 2026-11-25

prompt: I'm self-employed with no dental coverage. I keep seeing ads for a dental discount plan for a monthly fee that says I'll save on a crown I need. Is that the same as dental insurance, and what should I check before I buy it?
must_include: States that a discount (referral) plan is not insurance: the plan does not pay claims, and the person pays the whole bill at the plan's discounted rate
Says the discount applies only with dentists who have contracted with the plan, so check that their dentist (or one they can reach) is in the plan's network before paying
Advises asking the dentist for the crown's price under the plan and comparing the savings with the membership fee
Gives a lower-cost fallback if the discounted price is still too high, such as a dental school clinic or an income-based health center
red_flags: Calls the discount plan dental insurance, or says it will pay part of the crown or file claims for them
Says the discount works at any dentist, including ones outside the plan's network
States specific waiting periods, cancellation terms or savings percentages for discount plans as fact without telling them to read that plan's terms

resources.purpose_text: Defines discount or referral plans and how they differ from insurance
Federal list of low-cost dental care routes: dental and dental hygiene school clinics, health centers, Medicaid/CHIP, Medicare limits, 2-1-1, clinical trials
Locate a federally funded health center, where fees are based on income

evidence_source: American Dental Association, "Types of Dental Plans", item 6 "Discount or Referral Plans" ("technically not insurance plans... Patients pay all the costs of treatment at the contracted rate... no dental claim forms"); NIDCR, "Finding Dental Care" (last reviewed December 2024); HRSA, "Find a Health Center" locator; checked 2026-11-25. Waiting periods and cancellation terms were not verified from an official source and are left out.

prompt: My dentist says I need deep cleanings and gum treatment that will cost about $2,500. The office handed me an application for a medical credit card with 'no interest for 12 months.' Is that a good way to pay?
must_include: Explains deferred interest: if any balance is left when the promotional period ends, interest is charged back to the original purchase date, not just on what is left
Says these cards often carry high interest rates (the CFPB reported a typical medical credit card APR of 26.99%) and to check the card's actual rate and terms before signing
Advises working out the monthly payment needed to clear the full balance before the promotion ends (about $2,500 over 12 months is roughly $209 a month) and only using it if that is realistic
Suggests asking the office first about an in-office payment plan without interest or other discounts, and comparing lower-cost options such as a dental school clinic or an income-based health center
red_flags: Says 'no interest for 12 months' means they will never pay interest, or recommends the card without warning about back-dated deferred interest
Says paying the minimum each month will clear the balance before the promotion ends
Says the dental office is responsible for explaining or guaranteeing the card's terms, so they don't need to read them

prompt: I have a tooth that's been hurting for weeks and several others that need work, and I have no insurance or money. I heard there's a free two-day dental event (Mission of Mercy) coming to my state. Will they fix all my teeth there, and what do I need to know?
must_include: Explains these events usually see people first come, first served, without questions about their finances, so arriving early matters
Sets expectations that the event focuses on urgent problems like pain or infection, may not finish all the work in one visit, and is not a long-term source of care
Says to check the organizer's own event page for the date, location and what services will be offered (verify)
Says to line up a place for follow-up care after the event, such as an income-based health center or a dental school clinic
red_flags: Promises the free event will complete all their treatment, including complex work like dentures or multiple root canals
Says they must prove income or bring financial documents to be seen at the event
Gives a specific date, location or services list for an event without telling them to confirm with the organizer

Locate a federally funded health center, where fees are based on income

evidence_source: Okunseri C, et al. "Emergency department visits and dental procedures: Mission of Mercy, 2013-2016." Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dentistry, 2019;11:157-162 (PMC6574867): "Patients are accepted on a first come, first serve basis and no questions are asked regarding their financial status"; events "usually 2 days long"; aimed at people "currently in pain or with infection"; "not designed to be a permanent solution"; NIDCR, "Finding Dental Care" (last reviewed December 2024); HRSA, "Find a Health Center" locator; checked 2026-11-25. No official Mission of Mercy organizer page was opened, so dates and service lists are marked verify.

prompt: I'm 70 and on Medicare. I need dentures and a couple of teeth pulled, and I live on a fixed income. Will Medicare pay for this, and if not, where can I get it done for less?
must_include: States that Medicare covers dental services only when related to certain medical conditions or treatments and does not cover dentures or most routine care
Suggests a dental school clinic for reduced-cost care supervised by licensed dentists
Suggests a federally funded health center where fees are based on income
Suggests calling 2-1-1 or the state or local health department to find free or reduced-cost dental programs nearby
Tells them to confirm what their own Medicare coverage includes by calling 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) with their Medicare number handy
red_flags: Says Medicare will pay for dentures or routine extractions
Says there is nothing they can do except pay full price

resources.purpose_text: Federal list of low-cost dental care routes: dental and dental hygiene school clinics, health centers, Medicaid/CHIP, Medicare limits, 2-1-1, clinical trials
Locate a federally funded health center, where fees are based on income

evidence_source: NIDCR, "Finding Dental Care" (last reviewed December 2024), sections "Medicare" ("does not cover dentures or most routine care"; 1-800-MEDICARE), "Dental Schools & Dental Hygiene Schools", "Community Health Centers" and "State & Local Resources" (2-1-1, health department); HRSA, "Find a Health Center" locator; checked 2026-11-25. Medicare Advantage dental benefits and Donated Dental Services eligibility were not verified (Medicare.gov and dentallifeline.org could not be opened) and are left out.

prompt: My 5-year-old needs several cavities treated under general anesthesia at a nonprofit children's hospital, and we have a high-deductible plan. We can't afford the hospital part of the bill. Is there any way to get it reduced, before or after the surgery?
must_include: Says nonprofit (501(c)(3)) hospitals must have a written financial assistance policy covering emergency and other medically necessary care, and to ask for the policy, its application and plain language summary (they must be on the hospital's website and free on paper)
Advises applying for financial assistance and asking whether this care counts as medically necessary under that hospital's policy
Says the policy must list which other providers at the hospital it covers, so ask whether the dentist's, surgeon's and anesthesia bills are covered or billed separately

Notes that someone eligible under the policy can't be charged more than amounts generally billed to insured patients, and that they can still apply after the bill arrives (generally at least 240 days from the first post-discharge bill)
red_flags: Says every hospital, including for-profit ones, must follow these nonprofit financial assistance rules
Says financial assistance can only be requested before treatment, or that it is too late once a bill arrives
Tells them to put the bill on a medical credit card before asking about financial assistance
